podcast.title: Brain Surgery and Post-Stroke Speech (2005)
podcast.body: Less than a week after his hemorrhages, Edwin underwent brain surgery to relieve pressure in his skull. For weeks afterward, he could only utter four phrases: "Yes," "No," "Grace Maxwell" (his wife's name), and "The possibilities are endless." "for weeks afterwards, he could only say four things. Yes, no. Grace Maxwell, which is the name of his wife, and weirdly, the possibilities are endless."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cerebral Hemorrhages (February 18, 2005)
podcast.body: On February 18, 2005, during a BBC visit, Edwin Collins felt unwell, experiencing dizziness and nausea. Two days later, he was in intensive care after suffering a major cerebral hemorrhage, described by doctors as "catastrophic." He then suffered a second, equally catastrophic hemorrhage. "Two days later though, he was an intensive care having suffered a major cerebral hemorrhage, bad bleeding of the brain. And then another one. And both were described as catastrophic."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Documentary "The Possibilities Are Endless" (2014)
podcast.body: A documentary about Edwin Collins's recovery from his brain injuries, titled "The Possibilities Are Endless," was released in 2014. "And then there's the documentary from 2014 entitled Appropriately, The Possibilities Are Endless."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cerebral Hemorrhages and Stroke
podcast.body: On February 18, 2005, Edwin Collins experienced a series of major cerebral hemorrhages, or catastrophic brain bleeding, shortly after feeling unwell during a BBC interview. Within two days, he was in intensive care, and less than a week later, he underwent surgery to alleviate pressure on his skull. "Edwin had suffered a major cerebral hemorrhage, and then another one. And then another one. Catastrophic bleeding of the brain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continued Music Career Post-Stroke
podcast.body: Four years after his stroke, Edwin Collins resumed recording music. Although his right hand's impairment prevents him from strumming a guitar, he retains the ability to form chords. While he now walks with a cane and speaks with a stutter, his singing voice remains unaffected, and he continues to release records. "He does stutter when he speaks, but when he sings, there's no trouble at all. Four years after the stroke, he started recording music again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Falling and Laughing, the Restoration of Edwin Collins (Book)
podcast.body: This inspiring book chronicles Edwin Collins' journey to recovery from his brain aneurysm and stroke, authored by his wife, Grace Maxwell, who was instrumental in his rehabilitation. "If you're ever looking to read an inspiring book, his wife Grace is the author of Falling and Laughing, the Restoration of Edwin Collins."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Limited Post-Stroke Communication
podcast.body: Following his severe strokes, Edwin Collins' ability to speak was significantly impaired for weeks, during which he could only utter four distinct phrases: "yes," "no," the name of his wife, Grace Maxwell, and "the possibilities are endless." "For weeks afterwards, he could only say four things. Yes, no. The name of his wife, Grace Maxwell. And for reasons that no one can explain, the possibilities are endless."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mellower Disposition and Bird Watching
podcast.body: Edwin Collins reports that his experiences have made him a much more "mellow" person than he was before his stroke. Among his current great pleasures is bird watching, an activity he enjoys while continuing his musical endeavors. "Edwin walks with a cane, and he says he's much more male than he ever was. And one of the things that gives him great pleasure is bird watching, and he continues to release records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Miraculous Recovery Aided by Wife
podcast.body: Despite a poor prognosis, Edwin made a remarkable recovery, largely attributed to the unwavering support of his wife, Grace Maxwell. She developed a recovery method involving drawing and writing in notebooks, tasks Edwin had to perform left-handed because the strokes had rendered his right hand useless. "Prognosis was poor, but he pulled through largely because of the incredible support he got from his wife."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Comeback (After 4 Years)
podcast.body: It took four long years for Edwin Collins to slowly return to music. Although his right hand was impaired, preventing him from strumming a guitar, he could still form chords, and he eventually resumed recording, releasing a couple of new albums. "Slowly he was able to get back into music. It took four long years. He couldn't strum his guitar anymore because of that bum right hand, but he can still form chords."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recovery with Wife's Support
podcast.body: Despite a poor prognosis, Edwin recovered with the unwavering support of his wife, Grace Maxwell, who encouraged him to draw and write in notebooks with his left hand, as his right hand was rendered useless by the strokes. "His wife, and this was as close to a saint as you'll find, was there every step of the way. It was her idea to help his recovery by getting Edwin to draw."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Speech vs. Singing Anomaly
podcast.body: Following his strokes, Edwin experienced significant stuttering when speaking. However, remarkably, when he sang, his stutter completely disappeared. "He still has trouble speaking, Edwin stutters a lot. But when he starts to sing, there's not a stutter to be heard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Possibilities Are Endless (Documentary)
podcast.body: A documentary film was made about Edwin Collins' experience and recovery from his strokes and brain injuries, sharing his remarkable story with audiences. "There's also a documentary entitled The Possibilities Are Endless."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Wife's Book on Recovery
podcast.body: His wife, Grace Maxwell, documented Edwin's recovery journey in her book titled "Falling and Laughing, The Restoration of Edwin Collins." "Grace wrote a book about Edwin's recovery called Falling and Laughing, The Restoration of Edwin Collins, which is extremely good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Prominence in New Pop
xref.body: Culture Club, fronted by Boy George, was a prime example of a New Pop band. Their unique visual presentation, amplified by music videos, helped them become cultural phenomena in the early 1980s. "Think Boy George and Culture Club, ABC in their Sharp Tuxedos, Orange Juice, a band of Scotland featuring Edwin Collins, Asda Camer was another, Heaven 17 was still another."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scottish New Pop Band
xref.body: Orange Juice, a band from Scotland featuring Edwin Collins, was identified as part of the New Pop movement of the early 80s, characterized by diverse pop styles and strong visual elements, often propelled by music videos. "Orange Juice, a band of Scotland featuring Edwin Collins, Asda Camer was another, Heaven 17 was still another."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Visuals in New Pop
xref.body: Boy George, as part of Culture Club, embodied the visual aspect of New Pop, where artists' unique looks and music videos turned them into brief cultural phenomena in the early 80s. "Think Boy George and Culture Club, ABC in their Sharp Tuxedos, Orange Juice, a band of Scotland featuring Edwin Collins, Asda Camer was another, Heaven 17 was still another."
